Malfatti

GeometryCirclesTriangles
Game: This is a picture, not a game: three circles are fitted into a triangle so that each one touches the other two and two sides.
How to play: Drag A, B or C, or focus a corner and use the arrow keys. Tick the boxes to show the construction lines and press Reset to start over.
Look for the math

In 1803 Malfatti asked for three circular columns of the greatest possible volume to be cut from a triangular block of marble. He assumed the three circles must touch one another and each touch two sides of the triangle. Steiner later found a way to draw that triad with straight lines and circles; move a corner here and the construction follows it.

Steiner's recipe

Find the point I where the three angle bisectors meet. Draw the incircles of the three triangles IAB, IBC and ICA; the bisectors are common internal tangents of each pair. For each pair take the other common internal tangent. The three new lines meet at one point L. They cut out the quadrilaterals APLT, BMLP and CTLM, and the incircles of those quadrilaterals are the three Malfatti circles.

What the construction actually gives

The page says the quadrilaterals are inscriptible, meaning that each one has a circle touching all four sides. For a tangential quadrilateral the two sums of opposite sides are equal (Pitot's theorem):

AP + LT = PL + TA

The logic test checks the whole recipe on 166 triangles, and also compares every point with a second transcription of the applet's own methods. The circles touch each other and two sides each, the three tangents concur, and the Pitot sums agree to within the applet's pixel-scale rounding. For an equilateral triangle of side s the three radii come out exactly s(√3 − 1)/4, which the test confirms.

A quirk of the old picture

The article says the second tangents cross the sides at the points M, P, T. The Java applet instead puts those labels on the touch points of the three small incircles with the triangle's sides, and its second tangents run close to the angle bisectors, not through those touch points. This port follows the applet's labels and geometry; the wording on the old page is loose. Longer triangles also make the applet's tangent choice fall back to a whole-pixel approximation, so the tangencies are checked to drawing tolerance rather than to machine precision.

Not the best packing

The page's strongest claim is that Malfatti's circles do not solve the original marble problem. For a side-s equilateral triangle their total area is 3πs²(2 − √3)/8. Put the big incircle of radius s√3/6 in the middle and two circles of a third of that radius into two corners instead: their total area is 11πs²/108, about 1.36% more. Lob and Richmond gave this counterexample in 1929; Goldberg later argued, and Zalgaller and Los proved, that the Malfatti circles are never optimal. The test verifies the equilateral comparison exactly and surveys many other triangles; the universal "never" is a theorem from the cited work, not something a finite test can prove.

Tick "Incircles" and "Second tangents" and drag one corner towards a right angle: watch the orange tangent slide and the blue tangency points move while the three Malfatti circles stay touching.
